claim: The gem dealer behind the 'Black Taj' myth got a mythical death himself.

knots.passage: A longstanding myth holds that Shah Jahan planned a mausoleum to be built in black marble as a Black Taj Mahal across the Yamuna river. The idea originates from fanciful writings of Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, a European traveler and gem merchant, who visited Agra in 1665. It was suggested that his son Aurangzeb overthrew Shah Jahan before it could be built.
knots.hatnote: Guides still tell of a second, black Taj that was never built.

knots.passage: Tavernier is best known for his 1666 purchase of the 116-carat Tavernier Blue diamond that he subsequently sold to Louis XIV in 1668 for 120,000 livres, the equivalent of 172,000 ounces of pure gold, and a letter of ennoblement.
knots.hatnote: The storyteller was a gem dealer, and he had one famous stone.

knots.passage: The In Search of... episode "The Diamond Curse" repeats a persistent myth that Tavernier was torn apart by wild dogs because of the curse of a blue diamond (subsequently called the Hope Diamond) he had allegedly acquired through deception and murder.
knots.hatnote: Then his own story was rewritten.

knots.passage: In keeping with these scripts, according to the legend, Tavernier did not buy the Hope diamond but stole it from a Hindu temple where it had been set as one of two matching eyes of an idol, and the temple priests then laid a curse on whoever might possess the missing stone. Largely because the other blue diamond "eye" never surfaced, historians dismissed the fantastical story.
knots.hatnote: The curse needed a crime, so the legend gave him one.

knots.passage: The stories generally do not bear up to more pointed examination; for example, the legend that Tavernier's body was "torn apart by wolves" is inconsistent with historical evidence which shows that he lived to 84 and died of natural causes.
knots.hatnote: And a grisly death to match.

knots.passage: There was speculation that jeweler Pierre Cartier further embroidered the lurid tales to intrigue Evalyn Walsh McLean into buying the Hope Diamond in 1911.
knots.hatnote: So who benefits from a cursed diamond?

payoff: Tavernier gave the world an imaginary Black Taj; a diamond-curse legend later gave him an imaginary death.
caveats: Cartier's role in embroidering the curse is described as speculation on the Hope Diamond page.
